turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: The fact that Mr. Worthing's house in Belgrave Square is let by the year to Lady Bloxham is a matter of grave concern, as it suggests a most distressing lack of property ownership.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He wasn't aware, Mr. Worthing didn't tell him, that the house was let by the year to Lady Bloxham, but it's true he didn't own it, it was a bit of a complicated situation, really.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: It is a pity that Mr. Worthing did not think to mention this peculiarity of his circumstances when first presenting himself as a suitor for Gwendolen's hand.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: This is all such a ridiculous fuss over nothing, Mother, and it's really not fair to Jack to imply he's somehow deceitful or unsuitable just because of a little misunderstanding about a house.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned stern, and she declared, The notion that one can simply 'misunderstand' about owning a house is quite ridiculous, and she daresay, most ungentlemanly.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Well, it's not exactly that Jack was trying to deceive anyone, it's just that Mr. Worthing hadn't made it clear that he didn't own the house, and Jack hadn't known, really.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: This is simply absurd, Mother, Jack's made it clear he didn't know about the house, and it's not his fault Mr. Worthing didn't tell him.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack was dead tired, he thought, and he couldn't help but feel that the whole situation had been a great deal of confusion, a series of misunderstandings that no one could have anticipated.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's eyes narrowed as she regarded Jack, her voice dripping with disdain, as she pondered the absurdity of his situation, and she wondered, with a hint of incredulity, how a man could possibly expect to know the history of his own property if he was not even aware of its existence.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack was not trying to make excuses, he thought, but perhaps he could explain the circumstances more clearly, if Lady Bracknell would like that.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's expression turned stern, her voice dripping with disdain as she declared, This is a very serious matter, Mr. Worthing, and she was not impressed by his explanations so far.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's eyes narrowed as she regarded Jack, her voice dripping with disdain. The house's history, she thought, was of little consequence, but what was of considerable consequence was his personal history, and she found it singularly lacking. A spot of scandal, a hint of impropriety, would have been far more enlightening than this dull, respectable facade he presented.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He supposed he could provide some information about his mother, if that was what Lady Bracknell was getting at.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's eyes narrowed as she regarded Jack Worthing, her voice dripping with skepticism, as she pondered the curious circumstance of his mother, a most relevant one, if she was not mistaken.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He supposed it might be a bit of a shock, but he had always thought of his mother as a widow, and he had no idea she was actually a...a lady, if Lady Bracknell would like to clarify the situation.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's eyes widened in dismay, her voice dripping with disdain, as she pondered the implications of this most singular and distressing revelation, and how it cast a rather unflattering light upon Mr. Worthing's family's reputation.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He didn't know what Lady Bracknell meant by 'a lady', but he supposed it was some sort of...distinction, and he wasn't quite sure how it reflected on his mother or his family's reputation, and he was beginning to feel a bit...overwhelmed by all this.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: The audacity of this young man, pretending to be something he is not, and expecting Lady Bracknell to condone such a preposterous deception.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He was trying to explain that he had genuinely believed his mother was a widow, and he had no reason to doubt it, but he was starting to feel a bit flustered by all the questions, and he wasn't quite sure how to set the record straight.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: The audacity of this young man, pretending to be something he is not, is simply staggering. Does he not know that to be a gentleman one must be born, not made?

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
